questions.question: In a multi-agent pipeline, a downstream/receiving agent produces a wrong result because it never got the structured context it needed. Whose responsibility was that?
options: The coordinator/upstream agent's — it's responsible for passing structured context forward to the agent that needs it, not just handing off a bare task
The downstream agent's — it should have inferred the missing context on its own
It's nobody's fault, this is an expected agent failure rate
The user's, for not providing more detail in the original request

questions.question: A coordinator hands a subtask to a specialized agent but only passes a short task description, not the relevant prior findings. The specialized agent then produces an inconsistent result. Where's the root cause?
options: In the coordinator's handoff — it dropped structured context on the way down, not in the receiving agent's reasoning
In the receiving agent's tool selection
In the receiving agent's prompt engineering only
In the user's original request, since it wasn't specific enough

questions.topic: workflows vs. agents rule of thumb
questions.question: What's the rule of thumb for choosing a workflow over an agent?
options: Use a workflow when the precise series of steps is known ahead of time; use an agent when the steps aren't known and Claude needs to plan its own path with tools
Always prefer agents, since they're strictly more capable than workflows
Use a workflow only for single-step tasks and an agent for anything with more than one step
The choice depends only on which is faster to build, not on task predictability

questions.question: Claude is given a long prompt with many constraints and keeps partially ignoring some of them. Which workflow pattern actually fixes this, and why is it not routing?
options: Chaining — break the task into sequential steps and send narrow follow-up corrections; routing doesn't apply because there's nothing to classify/categorize here
Routing — classify which constraint is being violated, then forward to a specialized prompt for that constraint
Parallelization — run all the constraints as independent subtasks and aggregate
Evaluator-optimizer — since any correctness problem should default to a grader loop

questions.question: What's the parallelization workflow pattern, and what's a key benefit?
options: Split one task into independent subtasks that run concurrently, then join results in a final aggregator call — each subtask prompt stays focused, is easy to evaluate independently, and the pattern scales by adding/removing subtasks
Run the same prompt multiple times and pick the majority answer
Split a task into sequential dependent steps that must run in order
Have one Claude call classify input, then forward to a specialized downstream pipeline

questions.question: Per the course's guidance (using Claude Code as the example), how should tools given to an agent be designed?
options: Abstract and generic (e.g. bash, read, write) rather than hyper-specialized (e.g. a dedicated 'refactor' tool) — the agent combines generic tools to accomplish specific goals
As hyper-specialized as possible, one tool per exact task, to minimize ambiguity
Agents should not be given tools at all — only workflows use tools
Tools should always be paired 1:1 with each possible user request type

questions.question: Why does environment inspection matter for agents?
options: An agent needs a way to check the actual resulting state after (or before) an action, rather than just trusting what the tool call claims happened
It's only relevant for computer-use agents taking screenshots, not general-purpose agents
It replaces the need for tool descriptions entirely
It's a workflow-only concept and doesn't apply to agents

questions.question: What is the evaluator-optimizer workflow pattern?
options: A 'producer' generates output, a 'grader' checks it against criteria, and feedback loops back to the producer until the grader accepts the result
Two producers generate output independently and a human picks the better one
A single Claude call that both produces and grades its own output in one pass with no loop
Routing input to one of several specialized producers based on category

questions.question: What's the tradeoff agents make relative to workflows, per this chapter?
options: Agents trade reliability/testability for flexibility — they handle unanticipated inputs and can ask for more input, but have a lower success rate and are harder to test
Agents are strictly higher accuracy than workflows in every case
Workflows can handle unanticipated inputs better than agents
There is no meaningful tradeoff; the choice is purely stylistic
